key_terms.meaning: A 4-tuple G = (V, Σ, R, S): variables V, terminals Σ, rules R of the form A → α, start symbol S; every rule rewrites one variable.
A symbol that never appears on the left of a rule; it belongs to the final strings of the language.
A symbol that can be rewritten by rules; it stands for a whole sub-language.
The special variable S from which every derivation begins.
A rewriting instruction A → α, where A is one variable and α is a string of variables and terminals.
A step-by-step sequence of rewrites from S to a terminal string, written S ⇒ ... ⇒ w.
A tree whose root is S, internal nodes are variables, leaves are terminals, and each node's children spell the right side of a rule.
The string read left to right from the leaves of a parse tree.
A grammar in which some string has two different parse trees (or two leftmost derivations).
A language is inherently ambiguous if every grammar that generates it is ambiguous.
A variable A with A ⇒* ε, so it can vanish; the nullable set is found by repeating: A is nullable if A → ε or A → α with every symbol of α nullable.
A rule of the form A → B, with one variable on the right; it copies a variable without consuming input.
A symbol that is either not generating (cannot reach a terminal string) or not reachable from S; it can never appear in a successful derivation.
Every rule has the form A → BC (two variables) or A → a (one terminal); S → ε is allowed only if ε is in the language.
Every rule has the form A → aα, where a is a terminal and α is a string of variables; each step of a derivation reads one terminal.
In every CFL there is a pumping length p such that any string of length ≥ p splits as uvxyz with |vxy| ≤ p, |vy| ≥ 1, and uvⁱxyⁱz in L for all i ≥ 0.
A map h from an alphabet to strings; it extends to strings by h(a₁...aₙ) = h(a₁)...h(aₙ).
A triangular table T[i, j] holding every variable that derives the substring from position i to position j; the string is accepted if S is in T[1, n].
Four grammar classes by rule shape: type 0 unrestricted, type 1 context-sensitive, type 2 context-free, type 3 regular.
Rules αAβ → αγβ with γ ≠ ε; the context α, β stays fixed, so length never shrinks.

takeaways: A context-free grammar is just a finite set of rewriting rules; its language is every terminal string you can reach from the start symbol.
A derivation is the rewriting written as a line of steps; a parse tree is the same rewriting drawn as a tree, and a parser builds the tree.
A grammar is ambiguous when a string has two parse trees; a language is inherently ambiguous when no grammar for it avoids this.
Removing useless symbols, ε-productions and unit productions gives a smaller grammar for the same language.
Chomsky normal form (A → BC or A → a) and Greibach normal form (A → aα) fix the shape of every rule so proofs and algorithms have few cases.
The pumping lemma for CFLs says a long enough string repeats a variable on one root-to-leaf path, so the two pieces around the repeat can be pumped together.
CFLs are closed under union, concatenation, star, reversal, homomorphism and intersection with a regular set, but not under intersection or complement.
CYK decides membership in about n³ rule checks on a CNF grammar, and the Chomsky hierarchy grades grammars by how tightly a rule's two sides are tied.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for a formal definition followed by a worked derivation or parse tree, a simplification or normal-form conversion, and a pumping-lemma or closure argument, so show each step and name the rule used.

bank.q: Define a context-free grammar formally. Give a grammar for {aⁿbⁿ | n ≥ 1} and derive the string aaabbb, showing each rewriting step.
outline: State G = (V, Σ, R, S) with the four parts defined.
Give rules such as S → aSb, S → ab; variables and terminals listed separately.
Show S ⇒ aSb ⇒ aaSbb ⇒ aaabbb.
Explain why no string with a after b can be derived.

bank.q: Explain the difference between a derivation and a parse tree. Draw the parse tree for a string from a small grammar and read off its yield.
outline: Derivation: linear sequence of rewrites; parse tree: same rewrites as a tree.
Root is S, internal nodes variables, leaves terminals.
Children of a node spell the right side of one rule.
Yield is the leaf string read left to right; compare with the derivation's final string.

bank.q: Define an ambiguous grammar and an inherently ambiguous language. Give one ambiguous grammar for arithmetic expressions and show two parse trees for the same string.
outline: Ambiguity: one string, two distinct parse trees or two leftmost derivations.
Grammar with E → E + E | E × E | (E) | id.
Two trees for id + id × id showing different groupings.
Inherent ambiguity: every grammar for the language is ambiguous; state it is a property of the language, not one grammar.

bank.q: Define nullable variables, unit productions and useless symbols, and state why each can be removed without changing the language.
outline: Nullable: A ⇒* ε; compute by fixed-point iteration.
Unit production A → B copies a variable; replace by A → α for every B → α.
Useless: not generating or not reachable from S.
Removal keeps exactly the same terminal strings; mention order matters (generating and reachable first, then ε and unit).

bank.q: Take a grammar containing ε-productions, unit productions and useless symbols. Remove all three and write the final equivalent grammar, showing each intermediate grammar.
outline: Find generating symbols, then reachable symbols; delete the rest.
Compute the nullable set by repeating the nullable rule.
For each rule, add erased versions with nullable variables deleted, then delete ε-rules (keep S → ε only if needed).
Find unit pairs (A, B) with A ⇒* B by unit rules only; add A → α for each B → α and delete unit rules.
Present the final grammar and argue the language is unchanged.

bank.q: Convert the grammar S → aSb | ε (and one grammar with longer right sides) into Chomsky normal form. Show every intermediate step.
outline: Remove ε-productions, unit productions and useless symbols first.
Introduce new variables for terminals that appear with other symbols.
Break long right sides into binary rules using fresh variables.
Final rules only A → BC or A → a; restore S₀ → S and S₀ → ε if ε is in the language.

bank.q: Convert a given context-free grammar into Greibach normal form, explaining the substitution and ordering steps.
outline: Put grammar in CNF or clean form first.
Order variables A₁,...,Aₙ and remove left recursion / forward substitutions so rules start with a terminal or a later variable.
Substitute back so every rule begins with a terminal.
Final shape A → aα with α a string of variables; mention resulting grammar may grow.

bank.q: Use the CYK algorithm on a CNF grammar to test whether a given string of length 5 is in the language. Show the table contents.
outline: Verify grammar is in CNF.
Fill diagonal T[i,i] with variables A where A → aᵢ.
Fill longer substrings using T[i,j] = union over split k of variables A with A → BC, B in T[i,k], C in T[k+1,j].
Accept iff S is in T[1,n]; state the O(n³) cost.

bank.q: Use the pumping lemma for context-free languages to prove that {aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1} is not context-free.
outline: Assume L is a CFL with pumping length p.
Choose s = aᵖbᵖcᵖ, length ≥ p.
Split s = uvxyz with |vxy| ≤ p and |vy| ≥ 1; vxy can touch at most two of the three blocks.
Pump i = 2 to unbalance the counts; contradiction with equal counts.
Conclude L is not context-free.

bank.q: Explain how an ambiguous grammar for if-else in C creates the dangling-else problem. Give an unambiguous grammar or a disambiguation rule and justify it.
outline: Grammar S → if E then S | if E then S else S | other.
Two parse trees for if E1 then if E2 then S1 else S2.
Examiner wants the two trees drawn and the conflict located.
Disambiguate by matching else with nearest unmatched then, e.g. separate matched and unmatched statement variables.
Argue every string still parses and now parses uniquely.

bank.q: Show that context-free languages are closed under union, concatenation and Kleene star, and prove by a counterexample that they are not closed under intersection.
outline: Rename variables of the two grammars to avoid clashes.
Union: new start S → S₁ | S₂.
Concatenation: S → S₁S₂.
Star: S → SS₁ | ε (or S → S₁S | ε).
Counterexample: {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} ∩ {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}, not context-free.
Conclude non-closure under intersection; complement non-closure follows by De Morgan with union.

bank.q: Compare the four levels of the Chomsky hierarchy by rule shape, language class and accepting machine, with one example language for each.
outline: Type 0: α → β unrestricted, recursively enumerable, Turing machine.
Type 1: αAβ → αγβ, context-sensitive, linear bounded automaton.
Type 2: A → α, context-free, pushdown automaton.
Type 3: A → aB or A → a, regular, finite automaton.
Strict inclusions; give examples: regular a*, CFL aⁿbⁿ, context-sensitive aⁿbⁿcⁿ, and an unrestricted example.

bank.q: A language is suspected to be non-context-free. Explain when you would use the pumping lemma and when closure properties, and apply both to classify two example languages.
outline: Pumping lemma: direct contradiction on a single carefully chosen string; useful for languages with three or more linked counts.
Closure: intersect with a regular set, or use homomorphism and complement arguments, to reduce an unknown language to a known non-CFL.
Worked example 1: {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} by pumping lemma.
Worked example 2: {ww | w in {a,b}*} by pumping or by intersecting with a*b*a*b*.
State that closure properties prove non-membership only when the operation preserves CFLs; conclude carefully.

glossary.def: A finite non-empty set of symbols, usually written Σ.
A finite sequence of symbols from an alphabet; ε is the empty string.
A set of strings over an alphabet.
A grammar whose every rule rewrites a single variable, A → α.
A sequence of rewrites from the start symbol to a string.
A derivation in which the leftmost variable is rewritten at every step.
A tree showing how a string is derived, with variables inside and terminals at the leaves.
Any string of variables and terminals reached in the middle of a derivation.
A grammar giving some string two different parse trees.
A grammar in which every string in its language has exactly one parse tree.
A context-free language for which no unambiguous grammar exists.
A variable that can derive the empty string.
A rule A → B whose right side is a single variable.
A symbol that is not generating or not reachable from the start symbol.
A normal form where every rule is A → BC or A → a.
A normal form where every rule is A → aα, α a string of variables.
The constant p in the CFL pumping lemma; strings of length at least p can be pumped.
A property saying an operation on languages keeps the result inside the same class.
A symbol-to-string map extended to whole strings.
A dynamic-programming membership test for CFLs that needs the grammar in CNF.
A grammar whose rules αAβ → αγβ keep the surrounding context and never shorten the string.
The four-level classification of grammars into type 0, 1, 2 and 3.
